extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, AI-for-math researchers, proof-assistant developers, software engineers and potential contributors/beta-testers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and design criteria for producing and curating 'structured motivated proofs' to populate a public database for training AI and for human consumption; includes what counts as a valid entry, allowed proof-discovery moves, platform interaction constraints, and moderation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured motivated proof is generated by standard moves
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured motivated proof is one that is generated by standard moves. At any one moment one is in a certain state (a proof-discovery state), and there will be a set of possible moves that can take one from the current proof-discovery state to a new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion expects a formal-ish model of the mental state while solving a problem and a fixed menu of moves (logical moves, library extraction, instantiation, generating metavariables, asking related questions such as generalization/specialization). The post promises fuller detail later and gives examples of these moves; the project aims to capture proofs that can be produced by sequences of such moves rather than free-form stream-of-consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit proof-discovery state representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof-discovery state should represent variables, hypotheses, goals, and logical relationships between questions and proved results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may record that e.g. P1 is a special case of Q2, or that a positive answer to Q1 could create a counterexample to Q2. The platform will model not just written steps but also mental links between questions and proved results so moves operate on that structured state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow basic logical moves (forwards/backwards reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard logical moves such as forwards or backwards reasoning must be available as moves to change the proof-discovery state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from hypotheses of the form A and (A implies B) one may decide to deduce B. These are basic mechanical moves that should be part of the move set and, where appropriate, implementable by conventional programs rather than LLMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library extraction must be 'obvious'
rubrics_metrics.description: When extracting results from the library (premise selection), the extraction is allowed only if it is obvious given the context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule of thumb: a library extraction is obvious if it is one of the first things ChatGPT thinks of when given a suitable non-cheating prompt. Disallowed are library calls that appear irrelevant but then magically turn out to be helpful (these feel like 'rabbits out of hats'). Example: given a continuous-composition-looking situation, the intermediate-value theorem was one of ChatGPT's top suggestions and thus counts as an obvious library extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiations must be 'obvious' or generated from existing state
rubrics_metrics.description: When discharging an existential goal ⟂ there must be an obvious instantiation for the witness; obviousness can come from the term already being present in the proof-discovery state or by generating it via sanctioned moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed obvious instantiations include choosing a term already present, creating metavariables (introducing a new variable and proceeding to note properties it must satisfy), or trying an 'extreme' or 'simplest' element. The ChatGPT rule of thumb may be used to judge simplicity/obviousness. Highly surprising choices that can only be found after extended thought should be disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate metavariables as a sanctioned move
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of guessing a witness immediately, one may create a metavariable and change the goal to record properties that such a witness would need; generating metavariables is an allowed, explicit move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This models the tactic 'I'll try to prove there exists x by introducing a placeholder and deducing properties of it.' The idea is to document how the candidate would be narrowed down during the proof, making discovery steps explicit rather than hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization and specialization must be purely 'obvious' logical moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Related questions formed by generalizing or specializing the current target are allowed only when the move is an obvious, purely logical generalization or an obvious instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed: dropping a hypothesis or forming a clear special case. Disallowed: replacing a hypothesis by a non-obvious alternative (e.g., replacing 'twice differentiable' with 'upper semicontinuous' is not an obvious logical generalization). The generalization/specialization move should not introduce non-obvious creative leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallow 'rabbits out of hats' (highly surprising, unmotivated steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries must avoid steps that look like magical introductions of helpful but previously irrelevant objects or results — i.e., 'rabbits out of hats'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform and moderation aim to make it difficult to insert such unexplained leaps. If a step is only justifiable after a long hidden chain of thought, it should instead be broken down into admissible moves or excluded. The project gives the Ellenberg–Gijswijt polynomial-method example as something that feels like 'magic' because earlier papers hide the motivating steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: No free-text typing allowed in the interface (point-and-click constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intended interface prohibits typing in arbitrary formulas/data; users can only select existing text, click buttons, choose from drop-downs, and accept/reject 'obvious' suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint is deliberate: by preventing typing, the system forces generation of witnesses/objects via structured moves (selection, menu choices), which serves as a proxy for showing where an idea came from. Example: an existential witness must be chosen from selectable items or built by clicking choices rather than freely inputting a closed-form expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs in the database should be move-generated via the interface
rubrics_metrics.description: An entry is intended to be a proof that has been successfully generated using the point-and-click interface (i.e., as a sequence of moves), not a free-form retrospective narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to collect examples of proofs produced by the interface so the dataset reflects the move-level provenance the project seeks to train AI to emulate. The platform will log the sequence of moves as part of the entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entries should be structured accounts of discovery, not stream-of-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: While the database should capture discovery accounts, raw stream-of-consciousness submissions are unsatisfactory: they can be hard to remember, too person-specific, and risk being disorganized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'motivated proof' entry should focus on the mathematical reasons for a proof being discoverable and be formatted in the structured move framework, so that different users' accounts are comparable and machine-usable. Moderation/curation will help enforce this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and curation to ensure usefulness and detect cheats
rubrics_metrics.description: A team of moderators will check entries to ensure they are good additions (not routine or sneaking-in rabbits) and will curate the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every successful submission will be included; routine arguments that don't require motivation or submissions that sneak in non-obvious steps using allowed moves may be rejected. Moderators are expected to be paid and to adjudicate borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-in-the-loop oversight; formal verification not required initially
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs generated by the system are not expected to be formally verified; there will be a human in the loop to catch mistakes, and this flexibility is considered beneficial for capturing natural-language mathematical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that some moves (mechanical ones) could be implemented conventionally, while others (obvious library extraction, simplest example) are best done by LLMs; humans will validate output. Later integrations may provide formal proofs alongside motivated accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform technical requirements and features
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform should be web-based and convenient, support subsidiary proof states, allow selection of LaTeX subexpressions (not rendering as images), provide dependency diagrams and zooming, and make it easy to author and navigate proof-discovery states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current prototype limitations: single proof state only, LaTeX rendered as images, LLM handling of all moves. Desired features include multiple nested proof states (for generalizations/specializations), mixing LLM and conventional program moves (e.g., modus ponens handled mechanically), and UI elements to inspect dependency graphs of statements/questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid implementation of moves (LLM vs conventional program)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some moves are better implemented by conventional programs (mechanical, deterministic steps) while others are better handled by LLMs (obvious library extraction, suggesting simplest examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modus ponens is extremely mechanical and should probably be done by programmatic logic; 'provide the simplest example' or 'obvious library extraction' are better LLM tasks. The architecture should allow a mix and swapping/improvement of move implementations over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with proof assistants and autoformalization pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a path to integrate motivated-proof generation with proof assistants (e.g., Lean) and to create blueprints that can be autoformalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project hopes for an interface that can run Lean in the background so motivated natural-language proofs include formal Lean proofs. Another plan is to use the structured outputs to train autoformalization, enabling mathematicians to search for proofs without learning a formal language while their thoughts are autoformalized as they work.
